Her hands were almost clean. A shadow of brown remained in the creases of her knuckles. Her grandmother turned them over, said nothing, and kissed the back of each.

Half the bazaar was at the bridge. Mamadaliev put his heavy hand on her head for a moment, said the bata — may your hearth be warm, may your road be open — and stepped back before anyone could see his face.

The gendarme captain was polite and had a clipboard. He asked her name and wrote it the way the forms from Tash-Kömür told him to: Yusupova, Zuhra Abdukadyrovna. He turned the clipboard round so she could check the spelling. It was the name on her school certificates and in the shop ledger, and she had never once said it aloud.
“That’s right,” she said.

He lifted the pole himself. Her mother went under it with the bread, then her grandmother with her stick, then the cousins carrying the chest and the rolled felts of the dowry. Her father stood beside the sandbag hut in his grey suit and did not come forward. On the far side of the pole Zuhra turned. He nodded once, as a trader nods across the walnut rows when the price is agreed and there is nothing more to say. She nodded back the same way, because she had learned it from him.
Halfway up the empty road her grandmother stopped.
“About here,” said Kumushay. “This is where my father stood.” She looked back at the pole, and up at the riders. “Now it’s nobody’s. That’s new.”

At the bend a grey-bearded man, one of Kuchkar’s brothers, had a school exercise book open on a stone. If the Gendarmerie wrote down names, the elders had decided, then so would the riders. He did not ask her name. He wrote it in round Latin letters, Zuhra Abdukadyr kyzy, and turned the book round so she could check it.
“That’s right,” she said.
Alisher stood holding a white horse hung with red and white tassels. They lifted her onto it, the women began the song that goes up the valley ahead of a bride, and Alisher took the bridle.
A bride does not look back at the house she is leaving, or she will be homesick all her life.

She looked back. Her father was still beside the pole, small and grey, the bazaar behind him and somewhere beyond the haze the Uzbek frontier. He would not move until the bend took her out of sight. Then he would cross the bridge and open the shop, because a few walnuts were coming down at night by the paths below Kyzyl-Unkur, and someone had to buy them.
Twelve kilometres up, twelve kilometres down, the agreement said. It had sounded like a great distance.
It was four hundred metres. She could still see his face.

The maps had been printed in 1983 by the Main Administration of Geodesy and Cartography of the USSR Council of Ministers, and stamped secret in the top right-hand corner, and then, at some point in the 1990s, stamped again declassified in a different ink. They were the best maps anyone had. They were the only maps both sides would accept, because they had been made by neither.
Major Daniyar Kudashev had forty-one sheets to get through. On the morning of the ninth of September he was on sheet thirty-four, and it had taken three days.

The talks were held in a conference hotel on the southern edge of Bishkek, among apple orchards, with a view of the Ala-Too. The political delegations met upstairs, in the large hall with the flags. Bektur Zhumabek uulu sat at one end of the long table for the Front, and the man from Toktarov’s office sat at the other, and the Kazakh, Uzbek and Kyrgyz observers sat along the sides and wrote everything down and said almost nothing, each one careful, every morning, to put on the record that his presence did not affect his government’s claim. The UN mediators went up and down the room like waiters.
The military track met downstairs, in a room that had been a restaurant. The tables had been pushed together into one long table and covered with green baize, and on the baize lay the maps.

There were four of them on each side. Kudashev for the administration, with a captain from the Gendarmerie and two men from the new State Defence Corps who did not know how to read a contour line. For the Front, three clan commanders and a man named Kaimbek Ashyraly uulu, who had been a lieutenant of engineers in the territorial defence force until March of that year and had then gone up into the mountains with his whole company and his whole company’s trucks.

In 1992 Kudashev and Kaimbek had dug trenches together in the snow outside Kobozev, under the same captain, eating from the same pot. Neither of them mentioned this on the first day. On the second day Kaimbek said, as they sat down, “Your hands still shake,” and Kudashev said, “Yours still don’t,” and that was the only time either of them mentioned it.

The rule was simple, and the UN man had written it on a whiteboard on the first morning: The line shall follow the positions held by the forces of each party at 00:00 hours on 1 September 2007. Each side had brought its own record of where its men had been at midnight on the first. Where the records agreed, a line was drawn. Where they disagreed, the two sides argued, and then a line was drawn.

It was drawn with a pencil. A Koh-i-Noor, grade 4H, very hard, sharpened to a point with a razor blade. The UN man had insisted on the hardest pencil in Bishkek, so that the line would be fine and leave no room for argument.

On the first day Kudashev had done the arithmetic, because he was an engineer by training and could not help it. At one to one hundred thousand, one millimetre on the map is one hundred metres on the ground. The finest 4H line, drawn carefully on good paper, is about a fifth of a millimetre wide.
Twenty metres. Every line they drew was twenty metres wide on the ground, and nobody would ever know which side of those twenty metres it ran.
On the second day he redid the arithmetic, because the pencil was blunter than he had thought. Forty metres.

Sheet thirty-four covered a stretch of the Talas valley foothills where the plain runs up into the first folds of the Alatau, on the Kenkol fan. It showed a scatter of winter houses, a stream, two tracks, and a hamlet with eleven buildings marked in black, named on the map in Russian letters Dzhar-Bash. Jar-Bash. Head of the gully.

The records agreed about almost all of it. The Gendarmerie had held the plain. The Front had held the hills. Between them, at midnight on the first of September, there had been about a kilometre of ground that nobody had held, and the line would run through the middle of it. Kudashev drew it, lightly, in pencil, and Kaimbek watched him draw it and nodded, and the UN man initialled the corner of the sheet.
Then Kaimbek put his finger on the map, a little above the line, and said: “That’s a spring.”
There was a blue circle on the map, very small, with a blue thread running down from it to the stream. Beside it, in the tiny italic of Soviet cartographers, it said rodn. For rodnik. Spring.
“It’s on your side,” said Kudashev.
“It’s on our side,” Kaimbek agreed. “And that”—he moved his finger, a millimetre, below the line—”is the graveyard.”
Kudashev looked. Below the line, on the administration’s side, was a small rectangle with a cross-hatch in it, the Soviet sign for a cemetery. It was perhaps three hundred metres from the spring.

“Jar-Bash buries its dead below the spring,” said Kaimbek. “It always has. They carry the body down from the village, past the spring, and they stop at the spring and wash their hands, and then they go down to the graves. Then they come back up past the spring and wash again. That’s how it’s done there.” He took his finger off the map. “With your line, the spring is ours and the graves are yours. So now a family from Jar-Bash will wash their hands on our side, and cross your checkpoint with the body, and bury their father in the Special Economic Zone, and cross back, and wash again on our side. And at your checkpoint someone will want to see the dead man’s passport.”
One of the Defence Corps men laughed. Nobody else did.
They argued about it for most of the morning. Not angrily. Kudashev had been in angry rooms, and this was not one. It was more like two old carpenters arguing about a joint.

If they moved the line down, below the graveyard, the administration lost a strip of pasture and a track that its patrols used. If they moved it up, above the spring, the Front lost the spring, and the village would have to come down to the administration’s side for water. They could make a loop. The line could bend down around the graveyard like a finger, and leave it on the Front’s side. But then it would be a salient, and salients have to be watched, and a salient around a graveyard would be watched by two sets of men with rifles, all the time, over the dead.

At twelve they broke for lunch. Kudashev did not eat. He went out into the hotel orchard and smoked, which he had stopped doing in 1995, with a cigarette bummed from the Kazakh observer’s driver. The apples were ripe. Wasps were working the fallen ones in the long grass.
Kaimbek came out after a while and stood next to him and did not smoke.
“You know Jar-Bash?” said Kudashev.
“My wife’s mother is buried there.”
Kudashev nodded. He had thought it would be something like that.
“In 1992,” said Kaimbek, looking at the mountains, “outside Kobozev, there was that boy from Talas. The one with the accordion. You remember?”
“Erik.”

“Erik.” Kaimbek nodded. “We buried him where he fell. There was no time. We marked it with his rifle. Afterwards, when it was over, his mother came out from Talas to find him, and nobody could find the place. The ground was all dug over. All the snow had melted.” He was quiet for a moment. “She walked up and down that field for three days.”
Kudashev finished the cigarette.
“I’m not moving the line,” he said. “I can’t. I have instructions. Every metre is a metre.”
“I know.”
“But I’m an engineer. I can draw badly.”
Kaimbek turned his head and looked at him.

After lunch they went back to sheet thirty-four. Kudashev took the 4H pencil from the UN man’s tray, looked at it, and put it back. He took his own pencil out of his breast pocket instead, an ordinary HB from a stationery stall in the Osh bazaar, a soft one, with a worn point, and he redrew the line through the kilometre of no man’s land below Jar-Bash.

He drew it carefully, the way he had been taught at the institute in 1988, with the pencil held upright and the paper turned to meet it. Where the line passed between the spring and the graveyard it went soft and grey and a little thick, as soft pencil does on paper, about as wide as the blue thread of the stream.
The UN man leaned over and looked at it for a long time.
“That’s not very precise, Major,” he said.
“No,” said Kudashev. “Soviet paper. It takes the graphite badly.”

The UN man looked at Kaimbek. Kaimbek looked at the map. Then the UN man shrugged, the shrug of a man with seven more sheets to get through before the political delegations met at five, and initialled the corner.

On the ground, a soft HB line at one to one hundred thousand is about a hundred metres wide. It is wide enough for a spring, a path and a graveyard, and for a family carrying a body down from a village to walk the whole way without coming out of the line at either side.

When the joint survey teams came to mark the line on the ground, in the summer of 2009, they reached sheet thirty-four in July. They found the pencil line on the map, soft and grey between the spring and the graves, and argued about it for a day, and in the end set no pillar there at all, and wrote in their report Line indeterminate on source map, to be referred to the Joint Liaison Committee. The Joint Liaison Committee meets monthly at Kara-Oi. It has not yet reached Jar-Bash.

Kudashev retired from the State Defence Corps in 2013 as a lieutenant colonel. Kaimbek Ashyraly uulu still lives in the hills above the Talas valley, and is said to be a judge of the clan court there. They have not met again.
The families of Jar-Bash still bury their dead below the spring, and wash their hands on the way down, and wash them again on the way back, and nobody asks them for any passports at all.
From the El-Choro post on the crest of the dam you could see three things: the reservoir behind, the gorge in front, and the switchyard below.

The reservoir was a long grey lake between brown mountains, and that winter it was lower than anyone had ever seen it. The water had gone down and down all through the dry autumn, leaving a wide bare shore of mud and stones the colour of ash. Under the water, and now under the mud, lay the old floor of the Toktogul valley, where the Kökjal had kept their winter camps until 1974. Asylbek Jumagul uulu’s grandfather had been born down there. When the water dropped, the old people of Ozgörüsh walked out across the mud to look for the foundations of their houses, and some of them found them.
The gorge went down from the dam toward the Fergana valley, narrow, very deep, with the river at the bottom white even in January.

And at the foot of the dam, on a ledge blasted out of the gorge wall, was the switchyard: a fenced field of steel towers, transformers, insulators and humming wire, where the power from the turbines was gathered up and sent away down the lines to the cities. The Gendarmerie held the switchyard. The El-Choro held the dam. The ceasefire agreement, which Asylbek had never read, apparently said that this was a temporary arrangement under international supervision. It had been temporary for sixteen months.

There were six riders at the post on the crest, two at a time in eight-hour watches, with a yurt for sleeping and a concrete hut that had been an inspection office. Asylbek had the night watch in January and February because he was twenty-six and unmarried and his name had been drawn. He did not mind the dark. He minded the cold, which came up off the reservoir ice at night and went through felt and sheepskin as if they were paper.

Below, in the switchyard, the Gendarmerie had a post too: a white cabin by the gate, with a light in the window and a stovepipe, and a searchlight on a pole that they turned on and off at intervals for no reason he could understand. At night there were usually two of them.
One of them watched him.

Asylbek did not know his name. He was young, thin, with a Russian fur hat with the flaps down, and he had binoculars, and every night at some point he came out of the cabin and stood by the fence and raised the binoculars and looked up the face of the dam at the El-Choro post. For a long time. Then he went back in.

The first time, Asylbek put his hand on his rifle. The third time, he raised his own binoculars, an old Soviet pair that had been his uncle’s, and looked back. He could see the boy quite clearly in the light from the cabin: a long nose, red with cold; a cigarette; a face that was bored, and young, and very tired.
They looked at each other through the binoculars for perhaps a minute. Then the boy lowered his, and lifted a hand, and went inside.

The power cuts began in the cities in December. Asylbek heard about them on the radio, on the Talas stations that still came through at night: rationing in Talas, four hours a day; rationing in Nurzhan; schools closed; old people dying in the cold in the blocks. The radio said it was the tribal side’s fault, because the tribal side held the dam and was stealing the water. The radio from the other side, from the camps, said it was the cities’ fault, because they had drained the reservoir all summer selling power to Kazakhstan and now there was none left. The UN engineers who came up once a month in a white Land Cruiser said it was the drought, and the glaciers, and the old turbines, and a great many other things, and that they would put it in their report.
Asylbek knew only that the water was low and the boy in the switchyard was cold.
In the second week of January the boy’s cabin lost its power.

It was a joke, in a way. He was sitting in the middle of one of the biggest switchyards in Central Asia, among wires carrying enough electricity for half a country, and his own cabin had no light. Something to do with the rationing, or a fuse, or an order from somebody in Tash-Kömür. The window went dark. The searchlight stopped. The stovepipe kept smoking, so they still had wood, but the cabin was black at night, a black box at the foot of the white dam, and the boy no longer came out with his binoculars.
On the third night Asylbek took the paraffin lamp from the inspection hut, lit it, and set it on the parapet of the dam, at the place directly above the cabin, where it could be seen from below.
He did not know why he did it. He told the others afterwards that it was so that the gendarmes could see the El-Choro were watching. This was partly true.
At about two in the morning the cabin door opened. The boy came out and stood by the fence and looked up at the lamp for a long time. Then he raised his hand.
After that the lamp went on the parapet every night, and every night, at some point, the boy came out and raised his hand.

In February the boy left something by the fence. Asylbek saw him do it through the binoculars: a small packet, wedged into the wire mesh at the corner of the switchyard where the service track came up to the foot of the dam. The track was in neither side’s ground, or both. Asylbek walked down it at dawn, slowly, with his rifle slung behind him and his hands where they could be seen. In the packet was a carton of cigarettes, American, the good kind they sold on the air base, and nothing else. No note.
He took it. The next night he left something in the same place: a round of kurut, the hard dried yoghurt his mother made, wrapped in a cloth, and a handful of dried apricots from Ozgörüsh.

They never spoke. They never came down to the fence at the same time. They left things in the wire, at dawn, at dusk, for six weeks: cigarettes, kurut, a tin of Russian condensed milk, a pair of wool socks from the Ozgörüsh market, a newspaper from Talas so old it was nearly history, a sheepskin hat with flaps, better than the Russian fur one; in the last week, from the boy, the Russian fur hat itself, as if in exchange; and once a bar of Mexican chocolate with chilli in it that Asylbek did not like at all and ate anyway.
In March a horse came down the gorge.

It was an El-Choro horse, a young grey mare belonging to a Kökjal family camped in the hills above the reservoir. She had broken her tether in a storm and wandered for two days and come down the service track in the night, and in the morning she was inside the switchyard. She had got in through a gap in the fence where the snow had brought down a post, and she was standing among the transformers, eating the dry grass between the concrete footings, with forty thousand volts over her head.

From the crest of the dam Asylbek watched the gendarmes come out of the cabin. There were three of them that morning. One of them had a rifle and raised it, not at the mare, at the dam, at the El-Choro post, because a horse from the tribal side was inside the switchyard and nobody had a rule for that. Asylbek’s partner on the watch put his own rifle up. For a moment everything on the face of the dam was very still.
Then the thin boy pushed the gendarme’s rifle down with the flat of his hand.

He said something. He went back into the cabin, came out with a length of rope, and walked slowly through the transformers to the grey mare, talking to her. Asylbek could not hear the words. He could see the boy’s breath. The mare lifted her head and looked at him and did not run. He put the rope round her neck and led her, at a walk, back out through the gap in the fence and up the service track to the corner where they left the packets. There he tied the rope to the wire, loosely, with a bow, the way you tie a horse you mean somebody else to untie. He went back to the cabin without looking up.

Asylbek walked down and untied her. She was cold and frightened and not hurt. He led her up the track, across the crest of the dam, and up into the hills, and gave her back to the family, and told them she had come back on her own.

In July the Kurultai on the Aksay Plateau approved the Toktogul protocol. The Kökjal stood aside: they would not lay the whip against it, but they would not give their consent to it either, because it did not give them back their valley. The line moved. The dam, the reservoir, the town of Toktogul and the gorge passed to the Special Economic Zone. The El-Choro rode away from the crest of the dam on the morning of the twentieth of July, in a column, with the old men of Ozgörüsh standing at the roadside, and a Gendarmerie company drove up from Tash-Kömür the same afternoon and took over the inspection hut.
Asylbek left the paraffin lamp on the parapet when he went. It was not lit. He left it at the place directly above the cabin.

He never knew the boy’s name. He has thought of finding out, since. He could ask; there are people at the crossings who know people. But he has thought about it and decided that if he knew the name he would have to know other things too: where the boy was from, and what he thought about the Kökjal and the valley under the water, and whether he was the one who wrote in the Gendarmerie logbook for those six weeks, every night, nothing to report.

He would rather not. He has a Russian fur hat with the flaps worn thin that a gendarme left in the wire at the foot of the Toktogul dam in the winter of 2009. It is worse than any hat he could buy. He wears it every winter in the hills above the reservoir, when he goes out across the ice to his family’s old ground in the years the water is low.
Vera Kim spoke four languages, and in the Kenkol valley in March 2009 she was paid to speak all of them at once.

Russian to the Gendarmerie surveyor, Captain Lukin, who spoke nothing else. Iradi to the two men from the tribal side, an old herder named Kalnazar and his grandson, who were there to see that the line went where the map said and no further. English to the two United Nations officers, a Uruguayan major and a Bangladeshi captain, who were there to see that everybody saw. And Korean to nobody, under her breath, to her grandmother, who had been dead for six years and who was the only person she had ever told the truth to without translating it first.

She was twenty-eight. She had a degree in philology from Talas State University and a job with the UN mission at Kara-Oi that paid in dollars. Her mother said it was the best job any Kim had ever had. Her grandmother would have said that it was a strange job for a Korean, standing in a field telling Iradis where Irad ended, and then would have laughed her short, dry laugh, and gone on peeling potatoes.

The pillars were concrete. They came up the valley road from Talas on a flatbed truck, lying down in rows like the dead after a battle. Each was a metre and a half tall, square, painted white, with a black number stencilled on two faces, and a steel pin set in the top that marked the exact point. The survey team set one wherever the line crossed a road, a track or a stream, and wherever it changed direction. Between the pillars, in the valleys, it ran straight. On the ridges above, where no truck could go, they built cairns of stones instead.
Vera found the pillars sad. She could not have said why. They were only concrete.

On the fourth day, the eleventh of March, they set pillar 1,147 at a bend in the Kenkol stream, a little above the Kara-Bulak crossing, on a flat of grey gravel. Captain Lukin took his readings and argued with the map, and the UN major checked his readings and argued with Lukin, and Vera translated the argument back and forth, slowly, until it ran out. The grandson and the Gendarmerie driver dug the hole together and set the pillar in it with concrete from a bag, and they all stood round and looked at it.
Then old Kalnazar went down to the stream.

He came back with water in his cupped hands, a little, carefully, the way you carry water for a horse that has been ill. He walked round the pillar once, sunwise, and poured the water at its foot. Then from his coat he took a twist of paper with dried juniper in it, and a box of matches, and his grandson took off his hat and held it to shelter the match from the wind. The juniper caught and smoked. The old man carried it round the pillar, once more, sunwise, and stood in front of it with the smoke going up from his hand into the cold air, and began to speak.
The UN major looked at Vera.
“What is he doing?”

Captain Lukin was looking at her too, in a different way. Lukin was from Nurzhan. He had a lot of opinions about the tribal side, and he had given her some of them in the truck. He did not need the old man translated. He could see what he was doing. He wanted to see what she would do.
Vera listened.

It was a bata, a blessing. She had heard a hundred of them, at weddings, at funerals, at the feasts of her Iradi neighbours in Nurzhan. She knew the shape of them, the way they began with the sky and the earth and came down to the particular thing, the house, the child, the horse. This one began with the sky and the earth. Then it came down to the stone, and the line.

She could translate it in two ways. She knew that at once, standing on the gravel with the juniper smoke in her nose. She could give the major a sentence, He is saying a traditional blessing, which was true, and polite, and would go in the major’s notebook and stay there. Or she could give him the words.
The words were not polite.
Her grandmother had come to the Chu valley in the autumn of 1937, in a cattle wagon from Vladivostok, at the age of nine.

She had told Vera about it only once, near the end, when she was in the hospital in Nurzhan and had stopped speaking Russian and spoke only Korean, an old Korean that Vera understood about half of. The wagon took thirty-two days. Her little brother died on the way and was put out beside the track somewhere in Kazakhstan, with the others who had died, because the train did not stop long. At the end of the line they were let out onto the steppe in the Chu valley in October, with nothing, and told to build a collective farm.
They dug holes in the ground and lived in them. The first winter, half the people from the wagon died.

Her grandmother did not die because an Iradi woman from the nearest village, a widow with five children of her own, came every week to the edge of the dugouts with a sack. In the sack was bread. Sometimes there was only a little. Sometimes, near the end of the winter, it was mostly bran. The Iradi woman never said anything. She left the sack and went away and came back the next week. Her grandmother never learned her name.
“So you will be good to them,” her grandmother had said in the hospital, in the old Korean, holding Vera’s wrist hard. “Always. Whatever they do. They are the people who brought the bread.”
Vera translated the bata word for word.
She said it in English, plainly, a little behind the old man, and did not soften anything.

Stone, you did not ask to be put here. Men put you here. Men with papers. Remember that it was men. The water of this stream has run here since before the first horse. It will run here after you have fallen down. Stone, when the papers are forgotten, and the men who wrote them are forgotten, the water will still be here. Do not think you are a mountain. You are a stone with a number on it. Let the herds go past you. Let the brides go past you. Let the dead go past you. Stand here if you must, but do not stand in anyone’s way.

The UN major wrote it in his notebook. The Bangladeshi captain did not write anything. He looked at the old man for a long time with an expression Vera could not read, and then, to everyone’s surprise, he bowed his head.
Captain Lukin said, in Russian, to her and not to anyone else: “You didn’t have to give them all of that.”
“He said all of that,” said Vera.
“You could have given them less.”
“Yes,” said Vera. “I could have.”

Lukin looked at her. Then he looked at the old man, who had finished and was putting his matches away. Then he looked at the pillar. After a moment he did a thing she had not expected. He took off his own cap, the Gendarmerie cap with the badge, and held it at his side until the last of the smoke had gone.

The next morning the survey team was to go higher, up the military road toward the Kenkol Pass, to look at the line where it left the valley and climbed toward the crest. The road was still under snow in places. They had two vehicles: the Gendarmerie truck and the white UN Land Cruiser. Vera was assigned to the Land Cruiser, as she had been every day.

At seven in the morning, as they were loading, Kalnazar’s grandson came down from the tribal side’s camp with a message. His grandfather was ill in the night. The cold, his chest. He wanted the interpreter. He wanted to say something to her, he said, in his own language, before the team went up.
The UN major looked at his watch. Then he said she should go, and catch them up with the truck. The truck was going later anyway.
So Vera walked up to the tribal camp with the grandson, and found the old man sitting up in his felt in the yurt, coughing, and perfectly cheerful, and not very ill at all.
“I wanted to give you something,” he said. “For yesterday.”
He gave her a twist of juniper in paper, like the one he had burned at the pillar.
“For your house,” he said. “You are from Nurzhan. In Nurzhan they have forgotten how to do this. Do it for your house.”
She did not know what to say. She said thank you. She sat with him and drank tea, because you cannot refuse tea, and it took an hour, because it always takes an hour.

She was still in the yurt when they heard it: one heavy, flat sound from higher up the valley, toward the pass. It rolled down between the mountains and came back from the other side, and then there was nothing, not even birds.

The anti-tank mine had been in the road since 1992, or since 2007; the reports could never agree. It was under the snow, at a place where the road had been cleared and checked the autumn before, and checked again, and found clean. The Land Cruiser was the first vehicle to pass that spring.

The Uruguayan major and the Bangladeshi captain were killed at once. Their names are on a stone at Kara-Oi, by the gate of the mission headquarters. Vera goes there every March, on the twelfth, and stands for a while, and goes back to work.

She still works for the mission. She has translated, by her own count, some hundreds of meetings of the Joint Liaison Committee and its sub-committees, and some hundreds of blessings, and one wedding across a line. She keeps the twist of juniper from Kalnazar on a shelf in her flat in Nurzhan, by her grandmother’s photograph. She has never burned it. She does not know the right words for it, in any of her languages.

Pillar 1,147 is still standing at the bend of the Kenkol stream. The herds go past it in May and October. The paint is coming off, and the number on the upstream face is almost gone. Someone, she does not know who, ties a white ribbon round its top every spring.

My mother had not been up the Kara-Unkur valley since the summer of 2007, and she said she did not intend to go again. She said this often, in the tone of a woman explaining the price of something she had decided not to buy. The road was bad. The crossing took all morning. Her brother came down once a year for the holidays, which was enough. Her knees were not what they had been.

In August 2011 the talks at Kara-Oi broke down. You will remember it if you are Iradi. If you are not, I am not the person to explain it. There are better accounts, by people who understand the Joint Liaison Committee. I will say only that for a few weeks that summer it had seemed possible that the line might be talked away. Then the clan delegation walked out of the room over a fraction, and the radio played the same statement from both sides all evening, and it was not possible any more.

In October, on the morning the walnut harvest opened in the forest above Arslanbob, my mother came out of her bedroom in her good coat and her walking shoes, with an empty cloth bag under her arm, and said she was going up for the walnuts.
“Mama. It’s four hundred kilometres. Your knees—”
“My knees,” said my mother, “can sit in a bus.”

We took the night bus from Talas to Tash-Kömür and a marshrutka from Tash-Kömür along the farm belt to Bazar-Korgon. She slept most of the way with her head on my shoulder. I did not. I looked out of the window at the dark and thought about the bridge, which I had crossed every year since 2007 to see my uncle and she had not crossed once.

At the bridge there was a proper building now, with a flag and a computer, and a queue. My mother stood in it without complaining. When we reached the window the gendarme asked her name, and she gave it, the registered one, the one with the Russian ending, the one on her pension book. Then he asked her business.
“Walnuts,” she said.
He looked at her empty bag and let her through.

The four hundred metres of road beyond the building were exactly as I had always found them: grey, empty, the ditch running beside them, walnut leaves on the tarmac. She stopped halfway and stood for a long time.

“My father stood about here,” she said. “In 1974, when I went down to Talas to study. He walked me as far as here and went home.” She looked up the road at the stone hut and the riders at the bend. “It’s nobody’s now. Did you know that? Nobody’s.”
“I know, Mama.”
“I didn’t think you did,” she said, and walked on.

At the bend a young rider with an exercise book asked her name. She gave it in the other form, Japarkul kyzy, her father’s name, which I had never once heard her use in Talas. The rider wrote it down, looked at it, looked at her, and said, “You’re Mamyrbek’s sister.” It was not a question. He got off his horse and walked beside her, leading it, all the way up to the first houses.

She stayed four days in the forest above the village with her brother’s family, on their plot, sleeping in a felt tent under the walnut trees as she had done every autumn until she was twenty. I had to go back to Talas for my classes. When I came back up on the Friday to fetch her she had walnut-black hands to the wrist, the way every child in the valley has them in September, and she had not looked so well in years.

Her brother’s family gave her a sack to take down. Not her cloth bag. A full jute sack, forty kilos, the best of their plot, the thin-shelled kind. It took two of my cousins to carry it to the riders’ post.
“Sell it in the bazaar,” my uncle said. “You’ll get a good price this year. They say the Uzbeks are paying well.”
My mother looked at the sack, and then at him.
“No,” she said.

At the bridge the gendarme on the window was the same one as on Monday. He looked at the sack, and at my mother’s black hands, and at the form, and asked her what she intended to do with forty kilos of walnuts.
“Give them away,” said my mother.

He said that if she intended to sell them in the bazaar there was a form. She said that she did not. He said that if she was giving them away there was no form for that. She said that in that case she would not trouble him with it. He looked at her for a long moment. I think he was trying to decide whether she was mocking him. She was not. Then he stamped the paper and lifted the pole by hand.
She gave him the first handful.

He did not know what to do. He held them in his palm, five walnuts, still with a little black on them from her fingers. Then he put them in his jacket pocket and said, “Thank you, apa,” and went back into his building quickly, as if someone might have seen.

She gave walnuts away all the way through Bazar-Korgon. To the women in the dried-fruit rows. To the old men in front of the chaikhana, who knew her family and asked after her brother and told her she was a fool and took them. To the boys hanging round the marshrutka stand. To a family of Uzbek traders who were buying by the tonne and who laughed and then, when they saw she meant it, stopped laughing and took a handful each and thanked her in Uzbek, and she thanked them back in Uzbek, which I had not known she still spoke.
At the far end of the walnut rows, one trader, an old man with a ledger who was weighing walnuts into paper cones for the Tash-Kömür buses, would not take hers.
“I buy walnuts, apa,” he said. “I don’t take them.”
“These aren’t for sale,” said my mother.

He looked at her for a long time. He was, I learned afterwards, a man called Abdukadyr Yusupov, and his daughter had married up the valley in 2007, and he had not been past the bridge since. Then he nodded slowly, took one walnut from her, only one, and cracked it in his palm against another, the way traders do, and ate it standing there.
“Arslanbob,” he said. “The Kuchkar plots. Or near them.”
“Near them,” said my mother.

He wrapped the rest of her handful, the ones she had held out to him, in a paper cone from his stack, and gave them back to her for the bus. The paper was old and soft and grey. I did not notice until we were on the night bus, somewhere above the Fergana Gateway, with my mother asleep against my shoulder, that it was a photocopy. Part of a map. There were three faded lines on it, green and orange and blue, and across the back, where the bus’s reading light shone through, strips of yellowed tape where pieces of it had once been joined.
I do not know where he got it. I have thought about it since, and I am glad I did not ask.

That is the end of the stories. Twelve kilometres up, twelve down: the line is still there, and the pillars, and the crossings, and the men who write down names on both sides. Nobody has sold Irad. Nobody has bought it. It is not, as far as I can tell, any closer to being whole. I wanted to write something that would end better than that, and I could not.

My mother died in the spring of 2014, at home, in Talas. She asked to be buried in the valley. It took the family nine days to get the papers to bring her up the road, through the bridge at the foot of the hills, past the place where her father had stood, and up through the walnut trees to the old graveyard above the river. She had wanted to go there all along, and had told me, every time, that she never would.
I walked behind her the whole way. At the building I gave them my name, and at the bend I gave them my name again. I did not mind. It was the same name both times.
Iradi words are given in the modern Latin spelling. Most are in everyday use; a few belong to the church or to the valleys.
aka — elder brother; a respectful address to an older man.
aksakal — “white beard”; an elder. The aksakal kengeshi is a council of elders.
apa — mother; a respectful address to an older woman.
ata — father, grandfather; a respectful address to an old man.
bata — a blessing, spoken over a person, a journey, a house or a meal. It ends with omin.
bayge — a long-distance horse race, run at feasts.
biy — the chief and judge of a clan.
boorsok — small pieces of fried dough, served at every feast.
chaikhana — a teahouse.
Chong-ene — grandmother.
El-Choro — the clan militias of the tribal regions, organised in late 2007 from the fighting units of the Popular Front.
elechek — the white headdress of a married woman, put on the bride by her husband’s mother.
jandarm — a gendarme. Not a polite word.
kalpak — the tall white felt hat worn by men.
kalym — bride price, paid by the groom’s family: livestock, money and goods, often a riding horse.
kashysh — a priest of the Syro-Iradi Church.
kuda — the bond between the families of a bride and groom; also the in-laws themselves.
kurut — hard balls of dried, salted yoghurt.
Kyamta — the feast of the Resurrection.
kymyz — fermented mare’s milk.
malka — the holy leaven of the mountain parishes, said to descend from the bread of St. Janyl. It is given and never sold.
Morkhan — the black, bull-headed god of the old religion, whom the church identifies with the Devil. Black things and cattle are his.
omin — amen.
Qurbana — the Eucharist, in the East Syriac rite of the Syro-Iradi Church.
sep — a dowry: felts, bedding, a chest.
shyrdak — a rug of cut and stitched felt in two colours.
toi — a feast; especially a wedding.
tör — the seat of honour, opposite the door of a house or yurt.
Places and institutions

Bill of Sale ₍Satuu Kagazy₎ — the draft treaties, prepared in secret in the winter of 2006–07 by the government of Prime Minister Orozbekov with Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, under which Irad would have been dissolved and divided among them. Read out in Nurzhan on 25 February 2007.
Bishkek Ceasefire — the agreement of September 2007 that ended the main fighting of the Second Civil War and fixed the Qara-Chik line.
DRI — the Democratic Republic of Irad, proclaimed in Talas on 9 December 2006 and dissolved on 4 June 2007.
Gendarmerie — the Republican Gendarmerie, which guards the line and the highways on the ISEZ side.
ISEZ — the Irad Special Economic Zone, proclaimed in Nurzhan on 25 February 2007: the cities, the river valleys and the roads between them.
Joint Liaison Committee — the committee of officers from both sides, chaired by the United Nations, that meets monthly at Kara-Oi to settle incidents on the line.
Popular Front — the alliance of clan militias and strike committees that rose in March 2007 and stormed Talas on 4 June.
Qara-Chik line — the ceasefire line, about 1,890 kilometres long, between the ISEZ and the tribal regions.
UNMI — the United Nations Mission in Irad, established in October 2007, with its headquarters at Kara-Oi.

In the speech of the valleys, a single suffix, -ptyr, tells the listener that the speaker did not see a thing with her own eyes but has it from others: he came back, they say. The herders and the old women of these stories use it constantly. The author uses it at the moments when nobody in Irad can be sure what happened. English needs a whole clause to do what Iradi does in two letters, and I have not always found room for one. Where you feel a story stepping back from what it is telling you, that is usually where the suffix was.

The stories are written in the standard Iradi of the Talas valley, but the characters do not all speak it. Valentina Kravchenko speaks Russian; her granddaughter speaks the mixture of Iradi, Russian and English that Nurzhan calls Russocha. The herders of the Moiynkum say sh where Talas says ch. The people of the Fergana rim season their Iradi with Uzbek. Vera Kim thinks in Korean. I have not tried to reproduce any of this with accents or misspellings. Where it matters, the author tells you who is speaking which language, and I have left it to her.

I have kept a few words in Iradi because English has nothing that will stand in for them: kuda, kalym, bata, malka, toi. They are in the glossary. I have kept the patronymics as Iradis write them, -uulu for a son and -kyzy for a daughter, and the Russian-style surnames as the forms of the ISEZ write them. More than one story turns on the difference.

Where the author quotes a public document, such as the legend of a map, the terms of the ceasefire or a letter printed in the Talas Herald, I have used the English of the period where it exists, and my own where it does not.

I was in Chicago in 2007, where my family had gone in the territorial years, and I followed the war on a laptop, refreshing the Talas Herald website at three in the morning. Translating this book, I have learned a great deal about my own city that nobody had told me. I am grateful to the author for her patience with my questions, and for her answers, which were never what I expected.

Aidana Mukash kyzy
Talas, 2016

These stories took eight years to write and would have taken longer without the people who told me what they remembered, and the people who told me what they did not want to remember and then told me anyway. Most of them asked not to be named, and I have kept that promise.

I thank my editors at Arsha Books, who read the first of these stories in 2012 and asked for the rest, and who published them in a year when it was not yet clear whether anyone would. I thank the organisers of the Mor-Wave evenings in Talas, who let me read prose to a room that had come for music, and the room, which listened.

I thank the staff of the State Archives of Irad, who found me the 1983 maps; the reading room of Talas State University; the parish of St. Tomas, which kept the yellow cards; and the families of the Kara-Unkur valley and of Bazar-Korgon, on both sides of the bridge.
I thank Aidana Mukash kyzy, who carried these stories into English and asked me questions about them that I had never thought to ask.
My father taught me the language these stories are written in. My mother taught me the road. This book is theirs.

Aikokul Tursunbek kyzy was born in Talas in 1985. Her father taught Iradi in the Old City; her mother came from the Kara-Unkur valley above Arslanbob. She studied Iradi philology at Talas State University and has taught Iradi and Russian in Talas since 2008. Since 2011 she has written for the culture pages of the Talas Herald. On Eki Chakyrym is her first book. She lives in Talas.
About the Translator

Aidana Mukash kyzy was born in Talas in 1980 and grew up there and in Chicago, where her family moved in 1996. She studied English at the University of Illinois and returned to Talas in 2010. She works as an interpreter and teaches translation at Talas State University. This is her first literary translation.

back_cover: T w e l v e K i l o m e t r e s In the winter of 2006 a government in Talas drew up papers to sell the country. A translator kneels on a ministry carpet with a map she should never have seen. A night watchman signs a letter for the first time in his life. A priest blesses a hundred and thirty-nine horses and not one man. A boy from Semiz leads a horse with its saddle turned backwards. A walnut trader’s daughter walks four hundred metres of empty road between two posts, and gives her name twice.
